rule: Every case pairs a fixture (or an absent one) with its REQUIRED outcome. A fixture with no case here is not testable and is a defect in the pack; a case whose `fixture` is null has no file by construction and states its resolution in `env`.

placeholders.$SANDBOX: a temp directory the harness owns; nothing outside it is read or written
placeholders.$HOME: the harness's sandboxed home — never the real one; ~/MERIDIAN.md is $HOME/MERIDIAN.md

env_convention: A key absent from `env` is UNSET. A key present with a null value is explicitly unset. `default_file` names the fixture copied to $HOME/MERIDIAN.md, or null for none.

cases.law: spec §2.2 state A — absent leaves current single-root behaviour unchanged, and it is not an error
cases.kills: a build that fails loud on a missing config, which would brick the CLI on every machine's first run

cases.law: spec §2.2 state C — the operator stated an intent that cannot be honoured
cases.kills: the silent fallback to ~/MERIDIAN.md. `expect_not` is load-bearing: a build that falls back LOADS the default file's mount and looks perfectly healthy

cases.law: spec §2.3 — a directory is not a readable regular file; the operator's next action is identical to the missing-path case, so the reason word is the same
cases.kills: a build that tests only `exists()` and then fails deep inside the parser with an io error instead of a teaching refusal

cases.law: spec §2.1 — an empty value states no path, so rung 1 does not fire and the chain falls to rung 2
cases.kills: treating an exported-but-empty var as a stated path, which turns the commonest shell accident into a hard refusal

cases.law: spec §2.1 — whitespace-only is empty
cases.kills: an is_empty() check that a trailing space defeats

cases.law: spec §2.1 — rung 1 wins over rung 2
cases.kills: reading the default whenever it exists. Both files declare a `field-notes` mount, so asserting only that field-notes loaded passes on the WRONG file; the three-mount assertion is what discriminates

cases.law: spec §2.1 — rung 2 cannot be built, which is not the same as rung 2 resolving to nothing
cases.kills: collapsing an unresolvable default path into state A, which would silently disable the config plane in any environment that does not export HOME

cases.law: spec §2.2 state D — a clean parse declaring zero mounts is treated as the absent case, not as an error
cases.kills: a build that refuses an empty mount table, and a build that reaches state D through a different code path than state A (the nil-vs-empty bug)

cases.law: spec §5 — the minimal well-formed mount block
cases.kills: nothing on its own; it is the floor the other acceptances build on

expect.order: document order, and it is asserted

cases.law: spec §3.1, §5.1 — many blocks, mixed kinds, prose between them
cases.kills: THE load-bearing acceptance (S3-R8(c)). A build that refuses every config, or loads only the first block, or drops the git-folder because it has no `vault:`, satisfies every refusal case in this pack and fails only here. Also kills a reader that requires `vault:` unconditionally

cases.law: spec §5.3 — S3-R7's ratified mitigation must be EXPRESSIBLE, because ~/MERIDIAN.md cannot itself be attested
cases.kills: a schema in which the mount table's own integrity cannot be claimed at all. The pin must survive parse VERBATIM — a reader that normalizes, truncates to the @fp display form, or re-mints the token breaks the claim it exists to carry

tools.name: llm-wiki
tools.config:
entry: LLM_WIKI.md
  vault: field-notes
  nested:
    deeper: true

cases.law: spec §6, §6.1 — the declaration is parsed strictly; the payload is carried verbatim and never interpreted
cases.kills: a build that refuses an unknown tool `kind`, which would make a config invalid by REMOVING a tool. Also kills a build that parses the payload as YAML: the assertion is byte-verbatim carriage, indentation included

cases.law: spec §4 — unknown frontmatter keys are permitted and ignored, the shipped posture at crates/policy/src/convention.rs:311-314
cases.kills: a deny_unknown_fields frontmatter decode, which would refuse every config carrying Obsidian properties on the user's own entry page

cases.law: spec §3 — the machine surface is the frontmatter plus engine-language fenced blocks; everything else is prose the engine never parses and never refuses because of
cases.kills: THE anti-vacuity case. Four decoys: a ```yaml block with mount-shaped keys, a ```meridian-mount nested inside a four-backtick fence, an indented snippet, and inline code. A line-scanning reader loads two or more mounts here and passes every other acceptance in the pack. `mount_count` is asserted, not just membership

cases.law: spec §4, §8.1a — an absent construct points at line 1
cases.kills: a reader that treats frontmatter as optional. The file carries a perfectly well-formed mount block, so `expect_not` is what proves no partial mount table was loaded

cases.law: spec §4 — an unterminated frontmatter fence yields the same reason word as no frontmatter, because the outcome is identical: there is nothing to read
cases.kills: a reader that scans for a closing `---` and, failing, silently treats the whole file as frontmatter

cases.law: spec §4 — a frontmatter block that opens and closes but carries no keys is `missing-required-key` naming `type`, not `no-frontmatter`: neither no-frontmatter condition holds, since the file does open with `---` and the fence does close
cases.kills: a door that reads only the parse tree. The markdown parser mints no frontmatter node for an empty metadata block, so such a door refuses `---\n---` as `no-frontmatter` and tells the author their file `does not open with a closed --- frontmatter block` — false about bytes the author is looking at. Asserting the Fix clause is what makes the case fail on the message as well as the reason word; asserting the reason word alone would still pass a build that kept the old sentence under a renamed reason

cases.law: spec §4 — the refusal carries the parser's own message
cases.kills: a hand-rolled key:value frontmatter scanner, which reads `tags: [config, meridian` as a valid string value and never notices

cases.law: spec §4 — both engine-read keys are required, and that is what makes unknown-key tolerance safe
cases.kills: an Option<String> type field defaulting to `meridian-config`, which would make a typo of `type` invisible

cases.law: spec §4 — the engine must not guess which schema the bytes speak
cases.kills: defaulting an absent version to 1, which silently reinterprets a future-format file as v1

cases.law: spec §4 — the discriminator exists because MERIDIAN_CONFIG can aim the engine at any path
cases.kills: a reader that ignores `type:` and half-loads an ordinary page a mis-set env var pointed at

cases.law: spec §4 — refuse loudly, never guess a future format (LockError::UnsupportedVersion, crates/lock/src/lib.rs:132-134)
cases.kills: a reader that parses the v2 file with v1 rules because the blocks happen to look familiar. The file carries a valid-under-v1 mount block precisely so this is the trap it is

cases.law: spec §4 — a non-integer version is a type violation, not an unsupported version; the operator's fix differs
cases.kills: collapsing the two into one reason word, which tells a user with a typo to go upgrade

cases.law: spec §5.1, §8.1a — an absent block field points at the block's opening fence
cases.kills: reporting `field-out-of-order` because `path` arrived where `name` was expected — a refusal that sends the operator to reorder fields they did not write

cases.law: spec §5.1 — every declared field is READ; §1.3 D-f, the deliberate difference from the INDEX's lossy round-trip
cases.kills: an ignore-what-you-do-not-know reader. The human's bytes are the only source here, so a silently-ignored field is a silently-ignored intent

cases.law: spec §5.1, §8.1a — a duplicate points at the SECOND occurrence and names the first
cases.kills: last-wins and first-wins alike; both are silent choices about which of two stated intents the operator meant

cases.law: spec §5.1 — canonical order, one spelling per fact; the refusal teaches the order
cases.kills: an order-free HashMap decode. It is not a correctness bug on its own, which is why it is stated: two configs that differ only in field order would otherwise diff as different

cases.law: spec §5.2 — the charset is the complement of the address grammar's operator set, so no legal name can collide with an address operator
cases.kills: accepting any non-empty string as a name. A name containing `:` `#` `@` `/` or `.` would be bindable but unaddressable, and U3 would inherit a name it cannot parse

cases.law: kind-sweep 2026-08-13 — `kind:` left the schema; a stale line refuses through the unknown-field door with the removal remedy, exactly as `primary:` refused on an engine too old to know it
cases.kills: a build that silently tolerates the retired field, minting a compatibility window nobody ruled

cases.law: spec §5.3 — well-formed is exactly `model::fingerprint::parse_fingerprint` returning Some: four non-empty dot-separated fields
cases.kills: BOTH failure directions. A reader that accepts any string lets an unverifiable claim into the one mechanism that checks the mount table's integrity; a reader that checks for the literal `fp1.span2.b3.` prefix refuses a git-folder root's file-grain pin, which uses a different codec. Parse is codec-agnostic on purpose (crates/model/src/fingerprint.rs:99-103)

cases.law: spec §5.1 — a body line that is not `key: value` is refused; prose about a mount belongs beside the block, not inside it
cases.kills: a skip-blank-lines parser. It looks harmless and it is what erodes one-spelling-per-fact: once blanks are skipped, comments follow, then indentation, and the block grammar is a dialect

cases.law: spec §5.1, §8.1a — the fault is an absent closing fence, so the line is the block's opening
cases.kills: parsing to end-of-file. An unterminated engine block means the author's intent about where the machine surface ENDS is unknown, and guessing it silently extends the strict grammar over prose

cases.law: spec §5.1 — the mount table is the single authority for the three-way translation, and a map with two values for one key is not a map
cases.kills: a Vec<Mount> with no uniqueness check. The two blocks declare DIFFERENT paths and kinds, so a last-wins reader resolves `field-notes` to the archive — a cross-root ref silently reading the wrong tree

cases.law: spec §6.1 — the payload is engine-opaque; the DECLARATION is not
cases.kills: extending payload opacity to the block's shape, which would make `meridian-tool` an unparsed region rather than a declaration

cases.law: spec §6 — indentation is the only structural fact the engine needs from the payload: it is what makes the payload's extent unambiguous
cases.kills: a reader that swallows everything after `config:` to the closing fence. `vault: field-notes` at column 0 is exactly the shape of a field the engine WOULD read, so the ambiguity is real and not hypothetical

cases.law: spec §6 — names are keys for the same reason mount names are: a consumer resolving `llm-wiki` must get one answer
cases.kills: uniqueness enforced on mounts but not on tools, which is the likely asymmetry once mount uniqueness is written first

cases.law: spec §5.1 field 4 — the primary root is DECLARED, never derived: exactly one mount carries `primary: true`, and its position in the file means nothing
cases.kills: every derived-primary reader: mounts[0]-wins, first-vault-wins, last-wins. The designated mount is deliberately NOT the first block, so a mounts[0] fallback looks healthy on every other acceptance and fails only here

cases.law: spec §5.1 field 4 — the only legal value is the literal `true`; a mount that is not primary says so by carrying no `primary:` line
cases.kills: admitting `primary: false` as a legal no-op, which mints a second spelling for one fact — and with it a reader that treats ANY present value as designation, so `primary: false` designates

cases.law: spec §5.1 — the designation is a role exactly one mount may hold; two designations is a table-level defect like duplicate-mount-name, refusing the whole table, never a tie the parser breaks
cases.kills: first-designation-wins and last-designation-wins readers — both blocks are otherwise legal vaults, so a build that picks either one loads a healthy-looking table anchored to a tree the operator did not choose
